title: Reconstruction from Two Views: Linear Algorithms
blurb: The epipolar constraint, the essential and fundamental matrices, the eight-point algorithm and its four-fold pose ambiguity, triangulation and the multiple-view matrix, planar scenes and homographies — the largest and most reliably examined block of the course.

knowledge_points.title: The Epipolar Constraint and Epipolar Lines
knowledge_points.recap:
**Derivation (four steps, each worth a mark).** From $\lambda_1x_1=X$ and $\lambda_2x_2=RX+T$:
1. Eliminate $X$: $\lambda_2x_2=R(\lambda_1x_1)+T$.
2. Eliminate $T$ by taking the cross product with $T$ (i.e. multiplying by $\hat T$): $\lambda_2\hat Tx_2=\lambda_1\hat TRx_1$, because $\hat TT=T\times T=0$.
3. Project onto $x_2$: $x_2^\top\hat Tx_2=0$ since $\hat T$ is skew-symmetric, so the left-hand side vanishes.
4. Divide by $\lambda_1\neq0$:
$$\boxed{x_2^\top\hat TRx_1=0.}$$
**Geometric meaning.** $x_1$, $x_2$, and the baseline are **coplanar** — the constraint is the triple product $\langle x_2,T\times Rx_1\rangle=0$.
**Epipolar line.** For a fixed $x_1$, the set of admissible $x_2$ is the line $l_2\sim Ex_1$ (calibrated) or $l_2\sim Fx_1'$ (pixel coordinates). Writing $l_2=(l_1,l_2,l_3)^\top$, the line in the image is $y=-\tfrac{l_1}{l_2}x-\tfrac{l_3}{l_2}$.
**Practical use.** It reduces correspondence search from a 2D image search to a **1D search along a line**: for any pixel in the first image, its match in the second must lie on the corresponding epipolar line. This is what makes stereo matching tractable and what lets RANSAC reject outliers.
**Epipoles.** $e_1$ and $e_2$ are the projections of the other camera centre, i.e. the points where all epipolar lines meet. They satisfy $Ee_1=0$ and $e_2^\top E=0$ (likewise for $F$) — so the epipoles span the left/right null spaces.
**Worked example.** Pure translation $T=(5,4,1)^\top$, $K_1=K_2=I$, $R=I$. Then $E=\hat T=\begin{pmatrix}0&-1&4\\1&0&-5\\-4&5&0\end{pmatrix}$ and for $x_1=(40,30,1)^\top$: $l_2=\hat Tx_1=(-26,35,-10)^\top$, i.e. $-26x+35y-10=0$, or $y=\tfrac{26}{35}x+\tfrac27$.
**Uncalibrated case.** With intrinsics the constraint is $x_2'^\top K_2^{-\top}\hat TRK_1^{-1}x_1'=0$, i.e. $x_2'^\top Fx_1'=0$. If you are given a **normalised** point in image 1 but want the epipolar line in **pixel** coordinates of image 2, only $K_2$ enters: $l'\sim K_2^{-\top}\hat TRx_1$.
**2023 paper focus.** Planar correspondences obey $H=K(R-tn^\top/d)K^{-1}$ (sign depends on the plane convention). A homography has eight projective degrees of freedom and needs four non-degenerate point pairs.
**Line coimages and calibration.** A homogeneous line $l$ satisfies $l^\top x=0$. Under $x'=Kx$, it transforms contravariantly as $l'=K^{-\top}l$. In the opposite image, $l_1\sim E^\top x_2$ and $l_2\sim Ex_1$; geometrically the correct plotted line passes through the relevant epipole.

questions.q: Let $x_1,x_2$ be the observed 2D points of a 3D point $X$ with depths $\lambda_1,\lambda_2\neq0$, so that $\lambda_1x_1=X$ and $\lambda_2x_2=RX+T$. Derive the epipolar constraint.
questions.answer:
**Step 1 — eliminate $X$.** Substituting $X=\lambda_1x_1$ into the second equation:
$$\lambda_2x_2=R(\lambda_1x_1)+T.$$
**Step 2 — eliminate $T$.** Take the cross product of both sides with $T$, i.e. multiply by $\hat T$ (where $\hat Tv\equiv T\times v$). Since $\hat TT=T\times T=0$:
$$\lambda_2\hat Tx_2=\lambda_1\hat TRx_1.$$
**Step 3 — project onto $x_2$.** Multiplying from the left by $x_2^\top$ makes the left-hand side vanish, because $x_2^\top\hat Tx_2=0$ for the skew-symmetric matrix $\hat T$:
$$0=\lambda_1x_2^\top\hat TRx_1.$$
**Step 4 — divide by $\lambda_1\neq0$:**
$$x_2^\top\hat TRx_1=0.$$
questions.extend: Skipping the justification of why $x_2^\top\hat Tx_2=0$ costs half a point — it is the skew-symmetry result $z^\top Yz=0$ from Chapter 1.

questions.q: Describe briefly how the epipolar line can be used in practice.
questions.answer:
The epipolar line is used to **find correspondences**.
**How.** For any given pixel in the first image, the corresponding pixel in the second image is constrained to lie **on** its epipolar line. That turns a 2D search over the whole second image into a **1D search along a line** — dramatically cheaper and far less ambiguous.
**Also.** The same constraint is a consistency test: a putative match that lies far from the epipolar line is an **outlier** and can be rejected (this is the residual RANSAC scores).

questions.q: Two cameras differ only by a translation $T=(5,4,1)^\top$ (so $X_2=X_1+T$), with $K_1=K_2=I_{3\times3}$. What is the equation of the epipolar line associated with the pixel $x_1=(40,30)^\top$ of the first image?
questions.answer:
$y=\dfrac{26}{35}x+\dfrac{2}{7}$.
**Computation.** With $R=I$, $E=\hat T=\begin{pmatrix}0&-1&4\\1&0&-5\\-4&5&0\end{pmatrix}$. In homogeneous coordinates $x_1=(40,30,1)^\top$, so
$$l_2=Ex_1=\begin{pmatrix}-30+4\\40-5\\-160+150\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}-26\\35\\-10\end{pmatrix}.$$
**Convert to slope-intercept.** $l_2^\top(x,y,1)^\top=0$ gives $-26x+35y-10=0$, hence
$$y=\frac{26}{35}x+\frac{10}{35}=\frac{26}{35}x+\frac27.$$
questions.extend: From $l=(a,b,c)^\top$: slope $m=-a/b$, intercept $=-c/b$. Do not forget to homogenise $x_1$ first.

questions.q: For the same two cameras ($T=(5,4,1)^\top$, $K_1=K_2=I$), what is the equation of the epipolar line associated with the pixel $x_1=(50,20)^\top$?
questions.answer:
$y=\dfrac{16}{45}x+\dfrac{20}{9}$.
**Computation.** $l_2=\hat Tx_1$ with $x_1=(50,20,1)^\top$:
$$l_2=\begin{pmatrix}0&-1&4\\1&0&-5\\-4&5&0\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}50\\20\\1\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}-20+4\\50-5\\-200+100\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}-16\\45\\-100\end{pmatrix}.$$
So $-16x+45y-100=0$, i.e. $y=\tfrac{16}{45}x+\tfrac{100}{45}=\tfrac{16}{45}x+\tfrac{20}{9}$.
questions.extend: Same $E$, different pixel — practise the $\hat T x_1$ multiplication until it is automatic; it appears in nearly every paper.

questions.q: Given two cameras related by a pure translation $T=(5,4,1)^\top$ with $K_1=K_2=I$, how do you decide which of several candidate pairs $(x_1,x_2)$ can be a pair of corresponding pixels?
questions.answer:
**Test the epipolar constraint** $x_2^\top\hat TRx_1=0$ (here $R=I$, so $x_2^\top\hat Tx_1=0$) for each candidate pair, using **homogeneous** coordinates $x=(u,v,1)^\top$.
**Efficient procedure.** Compute the epipolar line once per $x_1$: $l_2=\hat Tx_1$. Then a candidate $x_2$ matches iff $l_2^\top x_2=0$, i.e. iff $x_2$ lies exactly on that line.
**Worked example.** For $x_1=(40,10,1)^\top$, $l_2=\hat Tx_1=(-10+4,\ 40-5,\ -160+50)^\top=(-6,35,-110)^\top$, so the line is $-6x+35y-110=0$. Substituting $x_2=(20,\tfrac{46}{7})^\top$: $-120+35\cdot\tfrac{46}{7}-110=-120+230-110=0$ ✓ — this pair is consistent.
**Note.** The constraint is necessary but not sufficient: a point on the epipolar line need not be the true match (it could be any point along the corresponding ray).
questions.extend: Compute $l_2$ once, then just substitute each candidate — far faster than evaluating a full quadratic form per option.

questions.q: Two cameras are related by a pure translation $T=[2,2,-1]^\top$, with $K_1=\begin{pmatrix}3&0&0\\0&5&0\\0&0&1\end{pmatrix}$, $K_2=\begin{pmatrix}4&0&0\\0&4&0\\0&0&1\end{pmatrix}$. Let $x_1=[4,3,1]^\top$ be **normalised** coordinates in image 1. Which is the epipolar line in image 2 in **pixel** coordinates?
questions.answer:
$y=\dfrac56x-\dfrac43$.
**Computation.** Because $x_1$ is already normalised, $K_1$ does **not** enter; only $K_2$ maps the line into pixel coordinates:
$$l'\sim K_2^{-\top}\hat Tx_1=\begin{pmatrix}1/4&0&0\\0&1/4&0\\0&0&1\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}0&1&2\\-1&0&-2\\-2&2&0\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}4\\3\\1\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}5/4\\-3/2\\-2\end{pmatrix}.$$
**Slope–intercept.** $m=-\tfrac{l'_1}{l'_2}=-\tfrac{5/4}{-3/2}=\tfrac56$ and $b=-\tfrac{l'_3}{l'_2}=-\tfrac{-2}{-3/2}=-\tfrac43$.
questions.extend: Read the question carefully: normalised in image 1, pixels in image 2 ⇒ apply $K_2^{-\top}$ only. Applying $K_1^{-1}$ as well is the intended trap.

questions.q: Two cameras with known intrinsics $K_1,K_2$ are related by $X_2=RX_1+T$. Given a pixel $x_1'$ in image 1 and several candidate pixels $x_2'$, describe how to decide which can be a correspondence.
questions.answer:
**Use the epipolar constraint for uncalibrated cameras:**
$$x_2'^\top F x_1'=x_2'^\top K_2^{-\top}\hat TRK_1^{-1}x_1'=0.$$
**Procedure.** (1) Homogenise both pixels. (2) Build $F=K_2^{-\top}\hat TRK_1^{-1}$ — with $R=I$ this reduces to $K_2^{-\top}\hat TK_1^{-1}$. (3) Compute the epipolar line $l_2=Fx_1'$ once. (4) A candidate is admissible iff $l_2^\top x_2'=0$; if none satisfies it, the correct answer is "none of the other options".
**Equivalent calibrated form.** Normalise first, $x_i=K_i^{-1}x_i'$, then test $x_2^\top\hat TRx_1=0$ — the same computation, reorganised.
questions.extend: Each camera gets its **own** intrinsics: $K_1^{-1}$ on the right, $K_2^{-\top}$ on the left. Mixing them up flips the whole answer.

questions.q: Two cameras have intrinsics $K_1$ and $K_2$, and the relative pose mapping from camera 1 to camera 2 coordinates is $(R,T)$. State the epipolar constraint between two pixels $p_1\in\mathbb{R}^3$ and $p_2\in\mathbb{R}^3$ of image 1 and image 2 respectively, in homogeneous coordinates.
questions.answer:
$$p_2^\top\,K_2^{-\top}\,\hat TR\,K_1^{-1}\,p_1=0.$$
**Reading it.** $K_1^{-1}p_1$ and $K_2^{-1}p_2$ convert the pixels into normalised (calibrated) coordinates, where the calibrated constraint $x_2^\top\hat TRx_1=0$ holds; moving $K_2^{-1}$ across the transpose gives $K_2^{-\top}$ on the left.
**Equivalently** $p_2^\top Fp_1=0$ with the fundamental matrix $F=K_2^{-\top}EK_1^{-1}$ and $E=\hat TR$.
questions.extend: Each image gets its own intrinsics: $K_1^{-1}$ on the right, $K_2^{-\top}$ (inverse **and** transpose) on the left.

questions.q: Assume $[R,T]=\begin{pmatrix}1&0&0&5\\0&1&0&4\\0&0&1&1\end{pmatrix}$, $K_1=I_{3\times3}$ and $K_2=\begin{pmatrix}3&0&0\\0&2&0\\0&0&1\end{pmatrix}$. What is the equation of the epipolar line associated with the pixel $p_2=(40,30,1)^\top$ of the second image?
questions.answer:
**None of the other choices.**
**Computation.** With $R=I$ and $T=(5,4,1)^\top$,
$$\hat T=\begin{pmatrix}0&-1&4\\1&0&-5\\-4&5&0\end{pmatrix},\qquad F=K_2^{-\top}\hat TK_1^{-1}=\begin{pmatrix}0&-\tfrac13&\tfrac43\\ \tfrac12&0&-\tfrac52\\-4&5&0\end{pmatrix}.$$
The epipolar line in image 1 induced by $p_2$ is $l_1\sim F^\top p_2$:
$$F^\top p_2=\begin{pmatrix}0&\tfrac12&-4\\-\tfrac13&0&5\\ \tfrac43&-\tfrac52&0\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}40\\30\\1\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}11\\-\tfrac{40}{3}+5\\ \tfrac{160}{3}-75\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}11\\-\tfrac{25}{3}\\-\tfrac{65}{3}\end{pmatrix},$$
which is the line $11u-\tfrac{25}{3}v-\tfrac{65}{3}=0$, i.e. $v=\tfrac{33}{25}u-\tfrac{13}{5}$ — a **positive** slope, whereas every offered option has a negative slope. Hence none of them matches.
questions.extend: Before grinding through the arithmetic, check the sign of the slope: here it alone rules out all four candidates.

questions.q: Give a geometrical interpretation of the epipolar constraint.
questions.answer:
The three vectors $\overrightarrow{o_1X}$, $\overrightarrow{o_2o_1}$ and $\overrightarrow{o_2X}$ **form a plane** — i.e. the two viewing rays and the baseline joining the two optical centres are **coplanar**.
**Why the algebra says exactly that.** $x_2^\top\hat TRx_1=\langle x_2,\ T\times Rx_1\rangle$ is the scalar triple product of the three vectors, and a triple product vanishes precisely when the vectors are coplanar. That plane is the **epipolar plane**, and its intersections with the two image planes are the epipolar lines.
questions.extend: Coplanarity is also why the constraint is necessary but not sufficient: it fixes the plane, not the point along the ray.

questions.q:
Let $X_2=RX_1+T$ and $X_i=\lambda_i x_i$ in normalized coordinates.

1. Eliminate the depths and derive $x_2^\top\widehat T R x_1=0$. (5)
2. Give a geometric interpretation in terms of a plane and three coplanar vectors. (2)
3. Explain why the magnitude of $T$ cannot be recovered. (1)
questions.answer:
From $\lambda_2x_2=R\lambda_1x_1+T$, left-multiply by $x_2^\top\widehat T$. The terms $x_2^\top\widehat T x_2$ and $\widehat TT$ vanish, leaving
$$x_2^\top\widehat TRx_1=0.$$
Thus $E=\widehat TR$. Geometrically, $x_2$, $T$, and $Rx_1$ lie in one epipolar plane, so their scalar triple product is zero. Scaling $T$ only scales $E$, and the homogeneous constraint is unchanged; translation magnitude is unrecoverable from two calibrated views.
questions.extend: Generated set Q33-A: Deriving the epipolar constraint (8 credits). Cremers-style practice; not a past-paper citation.

questions.q:
Let $R=I$, $T=(1,0,0)^\top$, and $x_1=(0.2,0.1,1)^\top$.

1. Compute $E$ and the epipolar line $l_2=Ex_1$. (3)
2. Write the line equation in normalized image coordinates. (1)
3. Decide whether $x_2=(0.4,0.1,1)^\top$ satisfies the epipolar constraint. (2)
questions.answer:
With $R=I$,
$$E=\widehat T=\begin{bmatrix}0&0&0\\0&0&-1\\0&1&0\end{bmatrix},\qquad l_2=Ex_1=(0,-1,0.1)^\top.$$
The normalized-image line equation is $-v+0.1=0$, or $v=0.1$. Since $x_2=(0.4,0.1,1)^\top$ has second coordinate $0.1$, $x_2^\top Ex_1=0$ and it satisfies the epipolar constraint.
questions.extend: Generated set Q33-B: A numerical epipolar line (6 credits). Cremers-style practice; not a past-paper citation.

questions.q: Two calibrated cameras observe the same 3D point, with $X_2=RX_1+T$ and $X_i=\lambda_i x_i$. (a) Derive the epipolar constraint $x_2^\top E x_1=0$ with $E=\hat T R$. (b) How many degrees of freedom does $E$ have, and why is translation recoverable only up to scale? (c) Interpret $l_2=Ex_1$ and $l_1=E^\top x_2$ geometrically.
questions.answer:
**(a)** Substitute the projective depths:
$$\lambda_2x_2=\lambda_1Rx_1+T.$$
Left-multiplying by $x_2^\top\hat T$ gives
$$\lambda_2x_2^\top\hat T x_2=\lambda_1x_2^\top\hat TRx_1+x_2^\top\hat TT.$$
The left side vanishes because $x_2\cdot(T\times x_2)=0$, and $\hat TT=T\times T=0$, hence
$$\boxed{x_2^\top\hat TRx_1=0},\qquad E=\hat TR.$$
**(b)** Rotation contributes 3 DOF and the direction of $T$ contributes 2, so $E$ has 5 DOF. Scaling $T$ only scales the homogeneous equation and is therefore unobservable.
**(c)** $l_2=Ex_1$ is the epipolar line in image 2 on which $x_2$ must lie; it is the projection of the first viewing ray into image 2. Likewise $l_1=E^\top x_2$ is the corresponding line in image 1.

questions.q: For a noisy normalized correspondence $(x_1,x_2)$ and essential matrix $E$: (a) derive the geometric distance from $x_2$ to its epipolar line in image 2; (b) formulate a relative-pose refinement over $(R,T)$ using this distance and no 3D points; (c) explain whether this objective distinguishes the four decompositions of $E$.
questions.answer:
**(a)** The line is $l_2=Ex_1=(a,b,c)^\top$, hence
$$d(x_2,l_2)=\frac{|ax_2+by_2+c|}{\sqrt{a^2+b^2}}=\frac{|x_2^\top Ex_1|}{\sqrt{(Ex_1)_1^2+(Ex_1)_2^2}}.$$
**(b)** With $E=\hat TR$ and $\|T\|=1$, minimize
$$\min_{R\in SO(3),\,\|T\|=1}\sum_{j=1}^N\frac{\big((x_2^j)^\top\hat TRx_1^j\big)^2}{(\hat TRx_1^j)_1^2+(\hat TRx_1^j)_2^2}.$$
This has five pose unknowns regardless of $N$.
**(c)** All four pose candidates produce the same essential matrix and therefore the same epipolar lines and objective value. Triangulate points and apply the positive-depth (cheirality) test in both cameras to select the physical decomposition.

questions.q: A calibrated $640\times480$ camera has focal length $800$ px and centred principal point. Given $R_{1\to2}=\begin{pmatrix}-0.83&0.56&0\\-0.56&-0.83&0\\0&0&1\end{pmatrix}$, $t_{1\to2}=[0.1,0.5,0.1]^\top$, $p=[393,167]^\top$ in image 1, and candidates $q_a=[37,369]^\top$, $q_b=[235,331]^\top$ in image 2, which candidate is the likely correspondence? Show the epipolar test.
questions.answer:
Use
$$K=\begin{pmatrix}800&0&320\\0&800&240\\0&0&1\end{pmatrix}.$$
The normalised points are $\hat p=[0.091,-0.091,1]^\top$, $\hat q_a=[-0.354,0.161,1]^\top$, and $\hat q_b=[-0.106,0.114,1]^\top$. With
$$E=[t]_{\times}R=\begin{pmatrix}0.056&0.083&0.500\\-0.083&0.056&-0.100\\0.359&-0.363&0\end{pmatrix},$$
we obtain $\hat q_a^\top E\hat p\not\approx0$ but $\hat q_b^\top E\hat p\approx0$. Therefore **$q_b$** is the likely match.

questions.q: All matched points lie on the plane $\pi=[a,b,c,d]^\top$ expressed in camera frame 1. Express the image homography induced by this plane using $R_{1\to2}$, $t_{1\to2}$ and the common intrinsic matrix $K$.
questions.answer:
Let $n=[a,b,c]^\top$. With the plane convention $n^\top X+d=0$, the plane-induced homography is
$$H=K\left(R_{1\to2}+t_{1\to2}\frac{[a,b,c]}{-d}\right)K^{-1}=K\left(R_{1\to2}-\frac{t_{1\to2}n^\top}{d}\right)K^{-1}.$$

questions.q: Which statements about homography computation in 2D-2D geometry are correct?
questions.answer: **Correct: 2 only.** A projective $3\times3$ homography has eight degrees of freedom up to scale. Coplanar scene points obey the same homography. Each point pair gives two independent linear equations, so four non-degenerate correspondences are the DLT minimum.

options.text: A homography has five degrees of freedom.
2D-2D correspondences generated by coplanar 3D points can be fitted by one homography.
Each 2D-2D correspondence supplies one linear constraint on the homography entries.
DLT homography estimation requires at least five coplanar point correspondences.

questions.q: In the official two-camera bunny diagram, which labelled line in Image 2 is the epipolar line associated with the marked pixel $p$ in Image 1?
questions.answer: **Line (A).** The epipolar plane through the two camera centres and the 3D ray corresponding to $p$ intersects the second image plane in line (A). Equivalently, it must pass through the second epipole and the possible correspondence of $p$.

questions.q: Reproduce the 21RFB derivation of the coimage vector $l_1$ of the epipolar line in image 1 from a point $x_2$ in image 2, for $X_2=RX_1+T$, and state how $l_1$ transforms from normalised to pixel coordinates.
questions.answer: **(a)** In image 1, $l_1\sim e_1\times x_1$ because the line coimage is orthogonal to both homogeneous points. **(b)** Choose points on the two rays to write $l_1\sim(-R^\top T)\times(R^\top(\lambda x_2)-R^\top T)$. **(c)** Since $(R^\top T)\times(R^\top T)=0$, absorb sign and depth into scale: $l_1\sim(R^\top T)\times(R^\top x_2)=R^\top(T\times x_2)$. **(d)** Thus $l_1\sim R^\top\hat T x_2\sim E^\top x_2$ (sign is irrelevant in homogeneous line coordinates), where $E=\hat TR$. **(e)** If $x'=Kx$, then $l_1^\top K^{-1}x'=0$, so the pixel-coordinate line is $l'_1\sim K^{-\top}l_1$.

knowledge_points.title: The Essential Matrix
knowledge_points.recap:
**Definition.** $E=\hat TR$ — the middle part of the epipolar constraint $x_2^\top Ex_1=0$, for **calibrated** cameras (normalised coordinates).
**Degrees of freedom: 5.** Three from the rotation $R$ plus **two** from the translation $T$ — the scale of $T$ is not observable, so only its direction counts. (Equivalently: 9 entries − 1 scale − 3 constraints.)
**Characterisation (necessary *and* sufficient).** A non-zero $E\in\mathbb{R}^{3\times3}$ is an essential matrix **iff** its SVD has the form $E=U\Sigma V^\top$ with $\Sigma=\operatorname{diag}(\sigma,\sigma,0)$ for some $\sigma>0$ and $U,V\in SO(3)$. So $\sigma_1=\sigma_2$, $\sigma_3=0$, and hence $\operatorname{rank}(E)=2$ (**not** 3).
**Projection onto the (normalised) essential space.** Given any full-rank $A=U\operatorname{diag}(a,b,c)V^\top$ with $a\ge b\ge c>0$, replacing $\Sigma$ by $\operatorname{diag}(1,1,0)$ yields the closest normalised essential matrix $U\operatorname{diag}(1,1,0)V^\top$. This is step 2 of the eight-point algorithm.
**Useful identity.** $EE^\top=\hat TR(\hat TR)^\top=\hat TRR^\top\hat T^\top=-\hat T\hat T$, so $EE^\top=-\hat a\hat a$ for some $a\in\mathbb{R}^3$ — it depends only on the translation.
**Reading motion off $E$'s structure.** $E=\hat TR$ inherits the zero pattern of $\hat T$ and $R$. A camera constrained to translate in the $YZ$-plane and rotate about the $X$-axis has $R=\begin{pmatrix}1&0&0\\0&*&*\\0&*&*\end{pmatrix}$ and $T=(0,*,*)^\top$, giving $E=\begin{pmatrix}0&*&*\\ *&0&0\\ *&0&0\end{pmatrix}$. Conversely $E=\begin{pmatrix}0&a&0\\-a&0&0\\0&0&0\end{pmatrix}$ with $a>0$ corresponds to $R=I$ and $T=(0,0,\mp a)^\top$ — pure **forward or backward** motion along the optical axis, with no rotation (both signs give the same $E$ up to the overall sign, which is unobservable).
**Degenerate case: no translation.** If the two viewpoints coincide, $T=0$, so $E=\hat TR=0$ and the epipolar constraint becomes trivially $0=0$. **No rotation can be recovered from $E$** and the eight-point algorithm cannot be used — one must instead match directions directly (see the rotation-only knowledge point).
**2023 paper focus.** The five-point algorithm leaves a four-dimensional null space and imposes the essential constraints afterwards. A valid $E$ has singular values $(\sigma,\sigma,0)$; cheirality after triangulation selects one of four decomposed pose hypotheses.

questions.q: Which part of the epipolar constraint is the essential matrix $E$? How many degrees of freedom does $E$ have? Explain your answer.
questions.answer:
**The essential matrix is $E=\hat TR$**, so the constraint reads $x_2^\top Ex_1=0$.
**Degrees of freedom: 5.**
**Explanation.** Three degrees of freedom come from the rotation $R\in SO(3)$, and **two** from the translation $T$: although $T\in\mathbb{R}^3$, its **scale is not determined** (the whole reconstruction is only defined up to a global scale), so only its direction — two parameters — is observable.
**Cross-check.** $E$ has 9 entries; subtracting 1 for the overall scale and 3 for the constraints $\sigma_1=\sigma_2$, $\sigma_3=0$ leaves 5.
questions.extend: "Scale of $T$ is free" and "$\hat T$ has rank 2" are both worth partial credit — say the first explicitly.

questions.q: Let $E$ be a valid essential matrix with singular value decomposition $E=U\operatorname{diag}(\sigma_1,\sigma_2,\sigma_3)V^\top$, $\sigma_1\ge\sigma_2\ge\sigma_3$. Which of the following properties hold?
questions.answer:
**$\sigma_1=\sigma_2$** and **$\sigma_3=0$**.
**Why.** A non-zero $E$ is an essential matrix iff $E=U\operatorname{diag}(\sigma,\sigma,0)V^\top$ with $\sigma>0$ and $U,V\in SO(3)$: the two largest singular values coincide and the smallest vanishes.
**Rank.** Consequently $\operatorname{rank}(E)=2$ — so "$\operatorname{rank}(E)=3$" is false. Note that the option "$\operatorname{rank}(E)=2$" was not among the ticked ones on the paper, but it is an immediate consequence of $\sigma_3=0$; the two facts $\sigma_1=\sigma_2$ and $\sigma_3=0$ are the defining ones.
questions.extend: $E=\hat TR$: $\hat T$ is $3\times3$ skew-symmetric, hence rank 2, and $R$ is invertible — so $E$ has rank 2 no matter what.

questions.q: Let $E$ be a non-zero matrix in $\mathbb{R}^{3\times3}$. Give a necessary and sufficient condition for $E$ to be an essential matrix.
questions.answer:
A non-zero $E\in\mathbb{R}^{3\times3}$ is an essential matrix **if and only if** it has a singular value decomposition
$$E=U\Sigma V^\top\quad\text{with}\quad\Sigma=\operatorname{diag}(\sigma,\sigma,0)\ \text{for some }\sigma>0\ \text{and}\ U,V\in SO(3).$$
**In words:** two equal non-zero singular values and one zero singular value, with both singular-vector matrices proper rotations.
questions.extend: Say **singular** values, not eigenvalues — the marking scheme deducts for that swap.

questions.q: Let $E$ be a valid non-zero essential matrix and $F$ a valid non-zero fundamental matrix with SVDs $E=U_E\operatorname{diag}(\lambda_1,\lambda_2,\lambda_3)V_E^\top$ and $F=U_F\operatorname{diag}(\mu_1,\mu_2,\mu_3)V_F^\top$ (values ordered descending). Which property does **not** hold in general?
questions.answer:
**$\mu_1=\mu_2$ does not hold.** The equality of the two largest singular values is a property of the **essential** matrix only; the fundamental matrix $F=K_2^{-\top}EK_1^{-1}$ is distorted by the intrinsics, which destroys it.
**The others are all true.** $\operatorname{rank}(F)=2$ and $\mu_3=0$: $K$ has full rank, so $F$ has the same rank as $E$. $EE^\top=-\hat a\hat a$: indeed $EE^\top=\hat TR R^\top\hat T^\top=-\hat T\hat T$. $\lambda_1=\lambda_2$ and $\lambda_3=0$: the definition of an essential matrix.
questions.extend: Rank 2 is shared by $E$ and $F$; **equal singular values are not**. That single asymmetry is the whole question.

questions.q: Consider $E=\begin{pmatrix}1&0&0\\0&1&0\\0&0&0\end{pmatrix}$. State a full-rank matrix $A\in\mathbb{R}^{3\times3}$ that would yield $E$ when projected onto the normalised essential space. Justify your choice.
questions.answer:
Any diagonal matrix
$$A=\begin{pmatrix}a&0&0\\0&b&0\\0&0&c\end{pmatrix}\quad\text{with}\quad a\ge b\ge c>0$$
works.
**Justification.** $A=I\cdot\operatorname{diag}(a,b,c)\cdot I$ is already an SVD of $A$ (with $U=V=I\in SO(3)$). Projecting onto the **normalised essential space** means replacing the singular-value matrix $\Sigma$ by $\operatorname{diag}(1,1,0)$ while keeping $U$ and $V$:
$$I\operatorname{diag}(1,1,0)I=\begin{pmatrix}1&0&0\\0&1&0\\0&0&0\end{pmatrix}=E.$$
**$A$ must have full rank**, so $c>0$ strictly; the ordering $a\ge b\ge c$ is needed for $\operatorname{diag}(a,b,c)$ to be a valid (descending) singular-value matrix.
questions.extend: Projection onto the essential space never touches $U$ and $V$ — it only overwrites the singular values with $(1,1,0)$ (or $(\sigma,\sigma,0)$ for the unnormalised version).

questions.q: A camera's motion is constrained to the $YZ$-plane (centre $O=[0,t_1,t_2]$) and its rotation to a rotation about the $X$-axis (both in world coordinates). For $a,\dots,f\in\mathbb{R}$, which form does the essential matrix $E$ take for any two poses of this constrained camera?
questions.answer:
$E=\begin{pmatrix}0&a&b\\c&0&0\\d&0&0\end{pmatrix}$.
**Derivation.** A rotation about the $X$-axis fixes points on that axis, so
$$R=\begin{pmatrix}1&0&0\\0&*&*\\0&*&*\end{pmatrix}.$$
The translation is $T=-RO=-R(0,*,*)^\top=(0,*,*)^\top$, so its first component vanishes. Then
$$\hat T=\begin{pmatrix}0&*&*\\ *&0&0\\ *&0&0\end{pmatrix}\quad\Longrightarrow\quad E=\hat TR=\begin{pmatrix}0&*&*\\ *&0&0\\ *&0&0\end{pmatrix}.$$
**Reading it.** Constraining the motion removes degrees of freedom, and that shows up directly as a **zero pattern** in $E$ — which in turn reduces how many correspondences are needed to estimate it.
questions.extend: Whenever a paper constrains the motion, compute $\hat T$ first: its zero pattern usually survives the multiplication by $R$.

options.text: $E$ does not have a special structure, all entries can be non-zero

questions.q: Suppose you estimated an essential matrix with a linear algorithm and obtained $E=\begin{pmatrix}0&a&0\\-a&0&0\\0&0&0\end{pmatrix}$ with $a>0$. The camera coordinate system has $z$ towards the scene, $y$ down, and $x$ completing a right-handed system. Which type of motion did the camera undergo?
questions.answer:
**Forward or backward motion without rotation** — both are consistent.
**Derivation.** For a translation along the optical axis without rotation, $R=I$ and $T=(0,0,\mp a)^\top$, giving
$$E=\hat TR=\hat T=\begin{pmatrix}0&\mp(\mp a)&0\\ \pm a&0&0\\0&0&0\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}0&a&0\\-a&0&0\\0&0&0\end{pmatrix}.$$
**Why both signs.** $E$ is only defined up to scale — including sign — so $T$ and $-T$ give the same (normalised) essential matrix. Resolving forward vs backward requires the **cheirality** check on triangulated points, not $E$ alone.
**Why not the other options.** A sideways or upward translation would put non-zero entries in the third row/column of $\hat T$; a $90^\circ$ rotation about $z$ would destroy the antisymmetric $2\times2$ block structure.
questions.extend: Zeros in the third row and column of $E$ mean $T$ points along $z$ — the epipole is at the image centre, the classic forward-motion "expanding" flow field.

options.text: Sideways motion in positive $x$ direction, with $+90^\circ$ rotation around the $z$-axis
Upward motion with $+90^\circ$ rotation around the $z$-axis

questions.q: If the camera has the same position for the two viewpoints, can the essential matrix $E$ be used to estimate the rotation accurately? Justify your answer.
questions.answer:
**No.**
**Reason.** With the same camera position the translation is zero, $T=0$, and therefore
$$E=\hat TR=\hat0R=0.$$
The essential matrix vanishes identically, so the epipolar constraint $x_2^\top Ex_1=0$ is satisfied by **every** pair of points and carries no information. Consequently **no rotation can be estimated from such an essential matrix**.
**What to do instead.** Match ray *directions* directly: with $K$ known, $w=\frac{K^{-1}p_2}{\|K^{-1}p_2\|}$ and $v=\frac{K^{-1}p_1}{\|K^{-1}p_1\|}$ satisfy $w=Rv$, and two correspondences already determine $R$.
questions.extend: Zero translation ⇒ zero parallax ⇒ no depth and no epipolar geometry. This is also why pure-rotation sequences break structure-from-motion initialisation.

questions.q: A camera's motion is constrained to the $XZ$-plane (centre $O=[t_1,0,t_2]$) and its rotation to a rotation around the $Y$-axis (both in world coordinates). For $a,\dots,f\in\mathbb{R}$, which form does the essential matrix $E$ take for any two poses of this constrained camera?
questions.answer:
$E=\begin{pmatrix}0&a&0\\b&0&c\\0&d&0\end{pmatrix}$.
**Derivation.** A rotation about the $Y$-axis fixes the $y$-component, so $R=\begin{pmatrix}*&0&*\\0&1&0\\ *&0&*\end{pmatrix}$. The translation is $T=-RO=(*,0,*)^\top$, i.e. $T_2=0$, giving
$$\hat T=\begin{pmatrix}0&-T_3&0\\T_3&0&-T_1\\0&T_1&0\end{pmatrix}\quad\Longrightarrow\quad E=\hat TR=\begin{pmatrix}0&*&0\\ *&0&*\\0&*&0\end{pmatrix}.$$
**Compare with the $YZ$/$X$-axis version,** which gives $\begin{pmatrix}0&*&*\\ *&0&0\\ *&0&0\end{pmatrix}$ — the zero pattern follows the constrained axis, so work it out rather than memorising it.
questions.extend: Recipe: write down the zero pattern of $R$, deduce which component of $T$ vanishes, build $\hat T$, multiply.

options.text: $E$ does not have a special structure, all entries can be non-zero

questions.q:
For $E=\widehat TR$, prove

$$EE^\top E-\frac12\operatorname{tr}(EE^\top)E=0.$$

Use $RR^\top=I$, $\widehat T^\top=-\widehat T$, and $\widehat T^2=TT^\top-\|T\|^2I$. Clearly show the cancellation. (10)
questions.answer:
Using $RR^\top=I$ and $\widehat T^\top=-\widehat T$,
$$EE^\top=-\widehat T^2=\|T\|^2I-TT^\top.$$
Because $T^\top\widehat T=0$,
$$EE^\top E=(\|T\|^2I-TT^\top)\widehat TR=\|T\|^2E.$$
Moreover $\operatorname{tr}(EE^\top)=3\|T\|^2-\|T\|^2=2\|T\|^2$. Hence the second term is also $\|T\|^2E$, and
$$EE^\top E-\tfrac12\operatorname{tr}(EE^\top)E=0.$$
questions.extend: Generated set Q38-A: Proving the essential cubic constraint (10 credits). Cremers-style practice; not a past-paper citation.
tags: The 5-point algorithm and the Demazure constraint

questions.q: Given $E=U\operatorname{diag}(\sigma,\sigma,0)V^\top$, derive the two rotation candidates and the two signs of translation. Explain how to correct signs if a candidate rotation has determinant $-1$. Why are there four pose candidates? (9)
questions.answer:
Let
$$W=\begin{bmatrix}0&-1&0\\1&0&0\\0&0&1\end{bmatrix}.$$
The two rotation candidates are $R_1=UWV^\top$ and $R_2=UW^\top V^\top$; the translation direction is $t=\pm u_3$, where $u_3$ is the third column of $U$. Thus there are $2\times2=4$ pose candidates. If a rotation has determinant $-1$, flip one consistent SVD column/sign so that $\det R=+1$. Cheirality, not the algebra alone, selects the physical candidate.
questions.extend: Generated set Q39-A: Four pose candidates (9 credits). Cremers-style practice; not a past-paper citation.

questions.q: (a) Prove the Demazure constraint $EE^\top E-\frac12\operatorname{tr}(EE^\top)E=0$ for $E=\hat TR$. (b) Derive the RANSAC iteration bound for minimal sample size $s$, inlier ratio $w$, and success probability $p$. (c) Evaluate it for $w=0.5$, $p=0.99$ using the five- and eight-point algorithms.
questions.answer:
**(a)** Since $RR^\top=I$, $\hat T^\top=-\hat T$, and $\hat T^2=TT^\top-\|T\|^2I$,
$$EE^\top=-\hat T^2=\|T\|^2I-TT^\top.$$
Because $T^\top\hat T=0$,
$$EE^\top E=(\|T\|^2I-TT^\top)\hat TR=\|T\|^2E.$$
Also $\operatorname{tr}(EE^\top)=2\|T\|^2$, so the two terms in the Demazure expression cancel.
**(b)** One sample is all-inlier with probability $w^s$. Requiring $1-(1-w^s)^k\ge p$ gives
$$\boxed{k\ge\frac{\log(1-p)}{\log(1-w^s)}}.$$
**(c)** For $s=5$, $k\ge145$; for $s=8$, $k\ge1177$ (rounded up). The five-point solver needs roughly eight times fewer RANSAC samples.

questions.q: Let $E=U\Sigma V^\top$ with $\Sigma=\operatorname{diag}(\sigma,\sigma,0)$. Using the two $\pm\pi/2$ rotations about the $z$-axis, explain why the resulting translation matrices are skew-symmetric and the rotation candidates lie in $SO(3)$. Why are there four pose candidates, and how is the correct one selected?
questions.answer:
Let $W=R_z(\pi/2)$. The standard candidates can be written
$$R_1=UW^\top V^\top,\qquad R_2=UWV^\top,$$
with translation direction $T=\pm u_3$, equivalently represented by the two skew matrices obtained from $UW\Sigma U^\top$ and $UW^\top\Sigma U^\top$. Since
$$W\Sigma=\begin{pmatrix}0&-\sigma&0\\\sigma&0&0\\0&0&0\end{pmatrix},$$
its transpose is its negative, so conjugation by $U$ remains skew-symmetric. Orthogonality follows from $U,V,W\in O(3)$; choose the SVD column signs so that each candidate has determinant $+1$.
There are two possible rotations and two signs for translation, hence four combinations. Triangulate at least one correspondence for each and keep the unique candidate with positive depth in both cameras.

questions.q: Which statements about the five-point algorithm are correct?
questions.answer: **Correct: 3 and 4.** With five correspondences, the linear epipolar equations leave a four-dimensional null space, so the vectorised essential matrix is a linear combination of four known 9D basis vectors. Essential constraints then yield candidates. Decomposition produces four pose hypotheses, and triangulation/cheirality selects the physical one. A valid essential matrix has singular values $(\sigma,\sigma,0)$ and pose has 3 rotational plus 2 translational-direction degrees of freedom.

options.text: Essential-matrix decomposition assumes that all three singular values are equal.
The algorithm estimates two rotational and three translational degrees of freedom.
The algorithm linearly expresses the unknown vectorised essential matrix using four known 9D basis vectors.
After essential-matrix decomposition, triangulation is used to determine the correct rotation and translation.

knowledge_points.title: The Fundamental Matrix and Epipoles
knowledge_points.recap:
**Definition.** For uncalibrated cameras the epipolar constraint in **pixel** coordinates is
$$x_2'^\top Fx_1'=0,\qquad F=K_2^{-\top}\hat TRK_1^{-1}=K_2^{-\top}EK_1^{-1}.$$
**$E$ vs $F$.** Both have rank 2 and a zero smallest singular value. But $E$ has the extra structure $\sigma_1=\sigma_2$ (5 DOF); $F$ does **not** ($\mu_1\neq\mu_2$ in general) and has **7 DOF** (9 entries − 1 scale − 1 rank constraint). $E$ requires known intrinsics; $F$ does not.
**Epipoles.** $e_2$ is the image of camera centre 1 in image 2, $e_1$ the image of centre 2 in image 1. They are the null vectors:
$$Fe_1=0,\qquad e_2^\top F=0,$$
and every epipolar line in image 2 passes through $e_2$.
**Proof that $e_2^\top F=0$** (a full exam question):
(a) The position of camera $C_1$ in the frame of $C_2$ is $T$, so with depth $\lambda_1$ the epipole is $e_2=\tfrac1{\lambda_1}KT$, and $F=K^{-\top}\hat TRK^{-1}$ by definition. Hence $e_2^\top F=\big(\tfrac1{\lambda_1}KT\big)^\top\big(K^{-\top}\hat TRK^{-1}\big)$.
(b) $(KT)^\top=T^\top K^\top$ — the transpose of a product reverses the order.
(c) $K^\top K^{-\top}=I$ cancels.
(d) $T^\top\hat T=-(\hat TT)^\top$, using $\hat T^\top=-\hat T$.
(e) $\hat TT=T\times T=0$, so the whole expression is $0$.
**2023 paper focus.** $F$ is estimated directly from uncalibrated pixel correspondences. The epipole is the projection of the other camera centre, and all epipolar lines pass through it—not generally through the principal point.
**Depth-compatible correspondences.** The epipolar constraint is necessary but not sufficient: after a candidate lies on $l_2=Fx_1$, solve $z_2K_2^{-1}x_2=z_1RK_1^{-1}x_1+T$ and require positive depths (cheirality). A candidate on the line can still be physically invalid.

questions.q: Let $F$ be the fundamental matrix for cameras $C_1,C_2$ with common intrinsics $K$, let $T$ be the translation between the camera centres as seen in the frame of $C_2$, and let $e_2$ be the epipole in the second image. Prove that $e_2^\top F=0$, justifying each step.
questions.answer:
**(a)** $e_2^\top F=\Big(\tfrac{1}{\lambda_1}KT\Big)^\top\big(K^{-\top}\hat TRK^{-1}\big)$.
*Why:* the position of camera $C_1$ in the coordinate system of $C_2$ is $T$; with $\lambda_1$ its depth, the pixel coordinates of the epipole are $e_2=\tfrac{1}{\lambda_1}KT$. The second factor is the definition of the fundamental matrix.
**(b)** $=\tfrac{1}{\lambda_1}T^\top K^\top K^{-\top}\hat TRK^{-1}$.
*Why:* the transpose of a product is the product of the transposes in reverse order.
**(c)** $=\tfrac{1}{\lambda_1}T^\top\hat TRK^{-1}$.
*Why:* $K^\top K^{-\top}=I$, and the identity can be dropped from a product.
**(d)** $=-\tfrac{1}{\lambda_1}(\hat TT)^\top RK^{-1}$.
*Why:* $(\hat TT)^\top=T^\top\hat T^\top=-T^\top\hat T$, by skew-symmetry of $\hat T$.
**(e)** $=0$.
*Why:* $\hat TT=T\times T=0$.
questions.extend: $Fe_1=0$ follows symmetrically — the epipoles are exactly the right and left null vectors of $F$, which is why $\operatorname{rank}(F)=2$.

questions.q: Compare the essential matrix and the fundamental matrix: definition, degrees of freedom, singular values and when each is used.
questions.answer:
**Definition.** $E=\hat TR$ relates **normalised** (calibrated) coordinates: $x_2^\top Ex_1=0$. $F=K_2^{-\top}EK_1^{-1}$ relates **pixel** coordinates: $x_2'^\top Fx_1'=0$.
**Degrees of freedom.** $E$: **5** (3 rotation + 2 translation direction). $F$: **7** (9 entries − 1 overall scale − 1 rank-2 constraint).
**Singular values.** Both have $\sigma_3=0$, i.e. rank 2. Only $E$ additionally satisfies $\sigma_1=\sigma_2$ — the intrinsics destroy that symmetry in $F$.
**Use.** With known calibration, estimate $E$ (five-point or eight-point) and decompose it into $R$ and $T$ directly. Without calibration, estimate $F$; it still gives epipolar lines and epipoles, but the pose can only be recovered up to a projective ambiguity until the intrinsics are known.

options.text: $E$ has 5 degrees of freedom and $F$ has 7.
Both $E$ and $F$ have two equal non-zero singular values.

questions.q: (a) State the formula for the fundamental matrix $F$ in terms of the essential matrix $E$ and the intrinsic parameter matrix $K$. (b) State the epipolar constraint for uncalibrated cameras using $F$ and the image coordinates $x'_1,x'_2$ associated with the metric coordinates $x_1,x_2$ via the calibration matrix.
questions.answer:
**(a)** $$F=K^{-\top}EK^{-1}.$$
(With different cameras, $F=K_2^{-\top}EK_1^{-1}$.)
**(b)** $$x_2'^\top Fx_1'=0.$$
**Where it comes from.** The metric (normalised) coordinates are $x_i=K^{-1}x_i'$; substituting into the calibrated constraint $x_2^\top Ex_1=0$ gives $(K^{-1}x_2')^\top E(K^{-1}x_1')=x_2'^\top K^{-\top}EK^{-1}x_1'=0$.
questions.extend: The inverse-transpose on the left comes from moving $K^{-1}$ through the transpose of $x_2$ — that is the whole derivation.

questions.q: A camera matrix is $P=K[R|t]$, mapping $X$ to $x'$ via $PX\sim x'$; a pair $(P,P')$ with $P=[I|0]$ and $P'=[A|a]$ (with $K=K'=I$) is called canonical. (a) Let $F$ be a non-zero matrix and $(P,P')$ a camera pair. Show that if $P'^\top FP$ is skew-symmetric, then $F$ is the fundamental matrix of the pair. (b) Let $F$ be any $3\times3$ matrix and $S$ any skew-symmetric $3\times3$ matrix, and let $P=[I|0]$, $P'=[SF|e']$ with $e'$ the epipole satisfying $e'^\top F=0$ (assume $P'$ has rank 3). Prove that $F$ is the fundamental matrix of $(P,P')$.
questions.answer:
**(a)** $P'^\top FP$ is skew-symmetric **iff** $X^\top P'^\top FPX=0$ for all $X$ (a quadratic form vanishes identically exactly when its matrix is skew-symmetric — Chapter 2). Writing $x'=P'X$ and $x=PX$, that condition is exactly
$$x'^\top Fx=0\qquad\forall\ \text{corresponding }x,x',$$
which is the defining equation of the fundamental matrix of the pair $(P,P')$.
**(b)** Invoke (a): it suffices to verify that $P'^\top FP$ is skew-symmetric. With $P=[I|0]$ and $P'=[SF|e']$,
$$P'^\top FP=\begin{pmatrix}(SF)^\top\\e'^\top\end{pmatrix}F\begin{pmatrix}I&0\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}F^\top S^\top F&0\\0^\top&0\end{pmatrix},$$
using $e'^\top F=0$ to kill the bottom row. The block $F^\top S^\top F$ satisfies $(F^\top S^\top F)^\top=F^\top SF=-F^\top S^\top F$ because $S^\top=-S$, so the whole matrix is skew-symmetric. By (a), $F$ is the fundamental matrix of $(P,P')$.
questions.extend: The bridge "quadratic form $\equiv0$ $\iff$ matrix skew-symmetric" (Chapters 1–2) is what turns this projective statement into a one-line verification.

questions.q: Let $F$ be a matrix and $(P_1,P'_1),(P_2,P'_2)$ two canonical camera pairs for which $F$ is the fundamental matrix, with $P_1=P_2=[I|0]$, $P'_1=[A_1|a_1]$, $P'_2=[A_2|a_2]$. Prove that there exists a non-singular $4\times4$ matrix $H$ with $P_2\sim P_1H$ and $P'_2\sim P'_1H$.
questions.answer:
**(h) $\hat a_1A_1=\hat a_2A_2$.** Both pairs give the same $F$, and by the definition of the fundamental matrix for a canonical pair $[A|a]$ one has $F=\hat aA$; equating the two expressions gives $\hat a_1A_1=\hat a_2A_2\ (=F)$.
**(i) $a_2=u\,a_1$ for a non-zero scalar $u$.** From $F=\hat a_1A_1$ we get $a_1^\top F=a_1^\top\hat a_1A_1=0$, since $a_1^\top\hat a_1=0$. Likewise $a_2^\top F=0$. As $F$ has rank 2, its left null space $\ker(F^\top)$ is **one-dimensional**, so $a_1$ and $a_2$ are parallel: $a_2=ua_1$.
**(j) $A_2=u^{-1}\big(A_1+a_1v^\top\big)$ for some 3-vector $v$.** Substituting $a_2=ua_1$ into $\hat a_1A_1=\hat a_2A_2=u\hat a_1A_2$ gives $\hat a_1(uA_2-A_1)=0$, so every column of $uA_2-A_1$ lies in $\ker(\hat a_1)=\operatorname{span}\{a_1\}$, i.e. $uA_2-A_1=a_1v^\top$ for some $v$. Hence $A_2=u^{-1}(A_1+a_1v^\top)$.
**(k) Conclusion.** Take
$$H=\begin{pmatrix}u^{-1}I&0\\u^{-1}v^\top&u\end{pmatrix}.$$
Then $P_1H=[I|0]H=u^{-1}[I|0]\sim P_2$, and
$$P'_1H=[A_1|a_1]H=\big[u^{-1}(A_1+a_1v^\top)\ \big|\ ua_1\big]=[A_2|a_2]=P'_2.$$
So the two camera pairs are **projectively related** — which proves the theorem: a fundamental matrix determines the camera pair only up to a projective transformation of space.
questions.extend: This is the projective-ambiguity theorem: $F$ alone gives a reconstruction defined only up to a $4\times4$ homography — knowing $K$ is what upgrades it to metric.

questions.q:
Let $F\in\mathbb R^{3\times3}$ have rank 2 and let $e'$ satisfy $e'^\top F=0$. Set

$$P=[I\mid0],\qquad P'=[\widehat e'F\mid e'].$$

Show that this pair has fundamental matrix $F$ by proving the epipolar constraint for every corresponding projection. State a condition ensuring $P'$ has rank 3. (10)
questions.answer:
A point seen as $x$ by $P=[I\mid0]$ can be written $X=(x^\top,\lambda)^\top$. The second camera gives
$$x'=\widehat e'Fx+\lambda e'.$$
Let $y=Fx$. Then
$$x'^\top Fx=(e'\times y)^\top y+\lambda e'^\top y=0,$$
because a cross product is orthogonal to $y$ and $e'^\top F=0$. Hence every correspondence satisfies the epipolar constraint of $F$. With $e'\neq0$ and $\operatorname{rank}F=2$, this canonical construction generically gives $\operatorname{rank}P'=3$.
questions.extend: Generated set Q35-A: Constructing a camera pair from $F$ (10 credits). Cremers-style practice; not a past-paper citation.
tags: Any rank-2 matrix as a fundamental matrix

questions.q: (a) Show that the epipoles satisfy $Ee_1=0$ and $e_2^\top E=0^\top$, and state the rank consequence. (b) Starting from pixel coordinates $x_{i,px}=K_ix_i$, derive the fundamental matrix. (c) Compare the degrees of freedom of $F$ and $E$.
questions.answer:
Camera 2's center in frame 1 projects along $e_1\sim R^\top T$, so
$$Ee_1=\hat TRR^\top T=\hat TT=0.$$
Camera 1's center projects in image 2 along $e_2\sim T$, hence $e_2^\top E=T^\top\hat TR=0^\top$. Both null spaces are non-trivial, so $\operatorname{rank}E\le2$ (non-zero translation gives rank 2).
Substitute $x_i=K_i^{-1}x_{i,px}$ into $x_2^\top Ex_1=0$:
$$x_{2,px}^\top\underbrace{K_2^{-\top}EK_1^{-1}}_F x_{1,px}=0,$$
thus $F=K_2^{-\top}EK_1^{-1}$.
$F$ has 7 DOF: nine entries minus global scale and the rank-2 constraint. $E$ has 5 DOF because its two non-zero singular values must additionally be equal.

questions.q: Prove that every rank-2 matrix $F\in\mathbb R^{3\times3}$ is the fundamental matrix of some camera pair by choosing $P=[I\mid0]$ and $P'=[\hat e'F\mid e']$, where $e'^\top F=0$. Why does $F$ not uniquely determine the cameras?
questions.answer:
A 3D point whose first image is $x$ can be written $X=(x^\top,\lambda)^\top$. Its second image is
$$x'=P'X=\hat e'Fx+\lambda e'.$$
Writing $y=Fx$,
$$x'^\top Fx=(e'\times y)^\top y+\lambda e'^\top y=0,$$
because $e'\times y$ is orthogonal to $y$ and $e'^\top F=0$. Hence all corresponding projections satisfy the epipolar constraint of $F$.
The cameras remain projectively ambiguous. For any invertible $H\in\mathbb R^{4\times4}$, the cameras $(PH^{-1},P'H^{-1})$ together with points $HX$ produce exactly the same images. Calibration is needed to upgrade this projective reconstruction to a metric one (still up to global scale).

questions.q: Which statements about 2D-2D epipolar geometry are correct?
questions.answer: **Correct: 3 only.** Estimating a fundamental matrix does not require known intrinsics. An epipole is the image of the other camera centre. Every epipolar plane contains both camera centres, and the resulting epipolar lines pass through the epipole rather than generally through the image centre.

options.text: Computing the fundamental matrix from 2D-2D correspondences requires the camera intrinsics.
The epipole is the projection of a 3D point at infinity.
The epipolar plane passes through both camera centres.
Every epipolar line passes through the image centre.

questions.q: For two cameras related by pure translation $T=(-1,3,3)^\top$, complete 20RFB Problem 11: form the second-image epipolar line using $F=K_2^{-\top}\hat TK_1^{-1}$, justify the depth relation, and test the listed candidate correspondences.
questions.answer: **(a)** For the stated $K_1,K_2$ and normalised $x_1=(2,2,1)^\top$, the official line is $y=\tfrac{15}{14}x+\tfrac{40}{7}$. **(b)** In pixel coordinates $p_1=K_1x_1$, the line coefficients are $l_2=Fp_1=K_2^{-\top}\hat T x_1$. **(c)** Since $X_2=X_1+T$ and $X_i=z_iK_i^{-1}x_i$, one obtains $z_2K_2^{-1}x_2=z_1K_1^{-1}x_1+T$. **(d)** Substituting every candidate on $y=105$ into this vector equation yields no pair with positive depth in both cameras; therefore **None** is correct.

knowledge_points.title: The Eight-Point Algorithm
knowledge_points.recap:
**Three main steps.** Given $n\ge8$ point pairs $(x_1^i,x_2^i)$:
**1. Approximate $E$** by solving the linear system $\chi E^s=0$.
**2. Project onto the essential space** — enforce $\Sigma=\operatorname{diag}(\sigma,\sigma,0)$.
**3. Recover the displacement** $(R,T)$ from the essential matrix.
**Step 1 in detail.** Using $x_2^\top Ex_1=0$ and the Kronecker identity $u^\top Av=(v\otimes u)^\top A^s$, each correspondence gives one linear equation in the nine entries $E^s=[e_{11},e_{21},e_{31},e_{12},e_{22},e_{32},e_{13},e_{23},e_{33}]^\top$. Stacking $n$ of them gives $\chi\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times9}$ whose $i$-th row is
$$\big(x_2^ix_1^i,\ x_2^iy_1^i,\ x_2^i,\ y_2^ix_1^i,\ y_2^iy_1^i,\ y_2^i,\ x_1^i,\ y_1^i,\ 1\big).$$
**Solving in practice.** Take the SVD $\chi=U_\chi\Sigma_\chi V_\chi^\top$; $E^s$ is the **ninth (last) column of $V_\chi$**, i.e. the right singular vector of the smallest singular value — the minimiser of $\|\chi E^s\|$ subject to $\|E^s\|=1$ (Chapter 1).
**Why step 2 is needed.** The linear solution is **not** guaranteed to be an essential matrix: an essential matrix must have **rank 2** and **two equal non-zero singular values**, and nothing in $\chi E^s=0$ enforces that. So one replaces $\Sigma=\operatorname{diag}(\sigma_1,\sigma_2,\sigma_3)$ by $\operatorname{diag}\big(\tfrac{\sigma_1+\sigma_2}{2},\tfrac{\sigma_1+\sigma_2}{2},0\big)$ (or $\operatorname{diag}(1,1,0)$ when normalised).
**Step 3: four solutions.** Decomposing $E$ gives **four** $(R,T)$ candidates — two rotations (from $R=UR_Z^\top(\pm\tfrac\pi2)V^\top$) times two translation signs (the scale, hence the sign, of $T$ is free). Only **one** is physically valid; it is selected by the **cheirality condition**: triangulate the points and keep the solution for which the reconstructed 3D points lie **in front of both cameras** (positive depths).
**What the eight-point algorithm optimises.** It minimises neither the **reprojection error** (Euclidean distances between observed and projected points) nor the **photometric error** — it minimises an **algebraic** residual $\|\chi E^s\|$ with no geometric meaning. That is exactly why it is only used to *initialise* bundle adjustment.
**Minimal correspondences.** With known calibration: **5** in general (the five-point algorithm, matching the 5 DOF of $E$), **4** for a planar scene (homography). The eight-point algorithm uses 8 because it drops the non-linear constraints to stay linear.
**2023 paper focus.** Each match contributes one scalar epipolar equation. Eight matches give the linear $E/F$ estimate, with a norm constraint preventing the zero solution; a homography instead needs four matches because each supplies two equations.

questions.q: Give the three main steps of the eight-point algorithm.
questions.answer:
Given a set of $n\ge8$ point pairs $(x_1^i,x_2^i)$:
**1.** Compute an **approximation of the essential matrix** by solving the linear system $\chi E^s=0$.
**2.** **Project onto the essential space** — enforce the singular-value structure $\operatorname{diag}(\sigma,\sigma,0)$.
**3.** **Recover the displacement** $(R,T)$ from the essential matrix.
questions.extend: Step 2 is the one candidates forget — without it the "essential matrix" from step 1 generally is not one, and step 3 has no valid decomposition.

questions.q: Given $n\ge8$ point correspondences $\{x_1^i,y_1^i,x_2^i,y_2^i\}_{i=1}^n$, the eight-point algorithm solves $\chi E^s=0$ with $E^s=[e_{11},e_{21},e_{31},e_{12},e_{22},e_{32},e_{13},e_{23},e_{33}]^\top$. Write down the shape of $\chi$ and the expression for the row corresponding to the $i$-th correspondence.
questions.answer:
**Shape.** $\chi$ is an $n\times9$ matrix — one row per correspondence, one column per entry of $E$.
**Row $i$.**
$$\big(\,x_2^ix_1^i,\ \ x_2^iy_1^i,\ \ x_2^i,\ \ y_2^ix_1^i,\ \ y_2^iy_1^i,\ \ y_2^i,\ \ x_1^i,\ \ y_1^i,\ \ 1\,\big).$$
**Where it comes from.** Expanding $x_2^\top Ex_1=0$ with $x_j=(x_j,y_j,1)^\top$, or equivalently applying the Kronecker identity $x_2^\top Ex_1=(x_1\otimes x_2)^\top E^s$.
questions.extend: The row is exactly $x_1\otimes x_2$ — so the column order of $\chi$ must match the chosen stacking order of $E^s$.

questions.q: Once you are given $\chi$, how do you calculate $E^s$ in practice?
questions.answer:
Take the singular value decomposition $\chi=U_\chi\Sigma_\chi V_\chi^\top$; then $E^s$ is the **ninth (last) column of $V_\chi$**.
**Why.** We seek the non-trivial solution of $\chi E^s=0$, i.e. $\min_{\|E^s\|=1}\|\chi E^s\|$. As shown in Chapter 1, the minimiser is the right singular vector belonging to the smallest singular value — the last column of $V_\chi$. With noisy data $\chi$ has full rank 9 and this gives the least-squares approximation.
questions.extend: Last column of $V$, never of $U$: the unknown $E^s$ lives in the input space of $\chi$.

questions.q: Is the non-trivial solution of the linear system $\chi E^s=0$ guaranteed to be an essential matrix? Why?
questions.answer:
**No.**
**Why.** An essential matrix must have **rank 2** and **two equal non-zero singular values** ($\Sigma=\operatorname{diag}(\sigma,\sigma,0)$). The linear system $\chi E^s=0$ imposes neither condition — it only enforces the epipolar constraint on the given correspondences, so its solution generally lies outside the essential space.
**Remedy.** Project the solution onto the essential space by replacing its singular values with $\big(\tfrac{\sigma_1+\sigma_2}{2},\tfrac{\sigma_1+\sigma_2}{2},0\big)$ — step 2 of the eight-point algorithm.
questions.extend: Base the argument on the **structure of the essential space**, not on "numerical inaccuracies" — the latter only scores 1 of 3 points.

questions.q: How many possible solutions for $R$ and $T$ should we get from the essential matrix $E$? What are they? How can you rule out the incorrect solutions?
questions.answer:
**Four solutions.**
**Why.** There are **two possible rotations** (the decomposition of $E$ admits $R=UR_Z^\top(\pm\tfrac{\pi}{2})V^\top$) and **two possible directions for $T$** (since $T$ is only determined up to scale, including its sign). $2\times2=4$.
**Ruling them out.** Use the **cheirality condition**: the reconstructed 3D points must lie **in front of both cameras**. Triangulate the points for each of the four candidates and keep the one for which all (or the large majority of) points have **positive depth** in both views. The other three place points behind one or both cameras.
questions.extend: "Two for $T$" alone is not enough — say explicitly that the scale/sign of $T$ is free, and name the cheirality check.

questions.q: Which of the following statements about the eight-point algorithm is correct?
questions.answer:
**The eight-point algorithm minimises neither the reprojection error nor the photometric error.**
**Why.** It minimises the **algebraic** residual $\|\chi E^s\|$ subject to $\|E^s\|=1$ — a quantity with no direct geometric or photometric meaning. That is precisely why its output is used only to **initialise** a nonlinear refinement.
**Contrast.** Bundle adjustment minimises the **reprojection error** (Euclidean point distances); direct methods minimise the **photometric error** (intensity differences).
questions.extend: Algebraic vs geometric error is a recurring theme: linear algorithms are fast and closed-form but optimise the wrong thing.

options.text: The 8-point algorithm minimises the reprojection error (Euclidean distances between observed and projected points).
The 8-point algorithm minimises the photometric error (intensity differences between corresponding pixels).
The 8-point algorithm minimises neither the reprojection error nor the photometric error.

questions.q: You want to determine the 3D rigid-body motion (with unknown scale) between two images of the same static scene, knowing the intrinsic calibration. What is the minimal number of 2D-to-2D point correspondences needed **for a planar scene**?
questions.answer:
**4.**
**Why.** For a planar scene the two views are related by a **homography** $H\in\mathbb{R}^{3\times3}$, which has 8 degrees of freedom (9 entries up to scale). Each point correspondence gives 2 independent equations, so $4$ points give the 8 equations needed.
questions.extend: Planar ⇒ homography ⇒ 4 points. General ⇒ essential matrix (5 DOF) ⇒ 5 points.

questions.q: Same setting — known intrinsics, unknown scale. What is the minimal number of 2D-to-2D point correspondences needed **in general** (non-planar scene)?
questions.answer:
**5.**
**Why.** The essential matrix has **5 degrees of freedom** (3 rotation + 2 translation direction), so five correspondences suffice — this is Nistér's five-point algorithm.
**Contrast with the eight-point algorithm,** which needs 8 because it deliberately ignores the non-linear constraints $\sigma_1=\sigma_2,\ \sigma_3=0$ in order to keep the estimation linear.
questions.extend: Minimal number = degrees of freedom of the model. $E$: 5. $H$: 8 constraints ⇒ 4 points. $F$: 7 ⇒ 7 points.

questions.answer:
**It estimates a planar homography matrix.**
**Why.** The constraint being stacked is $\widehat{x_2}\,H\,x_1=0$ — the homography relation $x_2\sim Hx_1$ written as a cross product, which removes the unknown scale. Vectorising with the Kronecker identity gives $\big(x_1\otimes\widehat{x_2}\big)^\top H^s=0$, exactly the rows being appended. The solution is then the right singular vector of the smallest singular value, reshaped to $3\times3$.
**Why not the essential matrix.** The epipolar constraint $x_2^\top Ex_1=0$ is a **scalar** equation per correspondence, so its rows would be $x_1\otimes x_2$ (a $1\times9$ vector), not $x_1\otimes\widehat{x_2}$ (which contributes $3$ rows per point).
questions.extend: Spot the `hat`: a **scalar** constraint ⇒ essential/fundamental matrix; a **cross-product** constraint ⇒ homography (or a projection matrix).

questions.q: Seven point correspondences are used to estimate a fundamental matrix. (a) Why is the nullspace of the $7\times9$ design matrix generically two-dimensional? (b) How is the rank-two constraint imposed, and how many candidate matrices can result? (c) Why is this determinant constraint alone insufficient to characterise a calibrated essential matrix?
questions.answer:
**(a)** Seven independent epipolar equations give a design matrix $\chi$ of rank $7$, so by rank–nullity $\dim\ker(\chi)=9-7=2$. Let $F_1,F_2$ be the two matrices obtained from a nullspace basis.
**(b)** Every linear solution is $F(\alpha)=F_1+\alpha F_2$ up to scale. A fundamental matrix must have rank $2$, so impose
$$\det(F_1+\alpha F_2)=0.$$
The determinant is a cubic polynomial in $\alpha$, hence it yields one or three real candidates (at most three). Each must be scored against the correspondences, usually inside RANSAC.
**(c)** Rank two is the only intrinsic algebraic constraint on a fundamental matrix. An essential matrix must additionally have **two equal non-zero singular values**. Therefore $\det(E)=0$ alone does not guarantee $E\in\mathcal E$; a calibrated minimal solver must enforce the full essential-space constraints.
questions.extend: Nullspace dimension gives the family; the determinant turns that family into finitely many candidates. Do not claim that every rank-two matrix is essential.

questions.q: All matched 3D points lie on a plane $N^\top X=d$ and the calibrated cameras satisfy $\lambda_2x_2=R(\lambda_1x_1)+T$. (a) Derive the planar homography $x_2\sim Hx_1$ and state $H$. (b) Why are four point pairs sufficient to estimate $H$? (c) Which translation quantity is recoverable from $H$?
questions.answer:
Since $X=\lambda_1x_1$ lies on the plane,
$$\lambda_1N^\top x_1=d\quad\Longrightarrow\quad \frac1{\lambda_1}=\frac{N^\top x_1}{d}.$$
Dividing the second-view equation by $\lambda_1$ gives
$$x_2\sim Rx_1+\frac{T}{\lambda_1}=\left(R+\frac1dTN^\top\right)x_1,$$
so
$$H=R+\frac1dTN^\top.$$
The cross-product constraint $\widehat{x_2}Hx_1=0$ supplies two independent linear equations per correspondence. A $3\times3$ homography has $9$ entries but is defined up to scale, hence $8$ degrees of freedom; four pairs give the required $8$ independent equations.
Decomposing $H$ recovers the plane normal and **$T/d$**, not the metric translation $T$ separately: translation and plane distance share an unavoidable scale ambiguity.
questions.extend: The planar case needs fewer points because one homography maps every point on the plane; it is not an essential-matrix shortcut.

questions.q: For normalized points $x_1=(x_1,y_1,1)^\top$ and $x_2=(x_2,y_2,1)^\top$: (a) write the epipolar constraint as one row of a homogeneous linear system in the nine row-major entries of $E$; (b) explain why at least eight correspondences are needed; (c) state how the SVD estimate is projected onto the essential space.
questions.answer:
**(a)** If $e=\operatorname{vec}(E)$ in row-major order, one correspondence gives
$$\big(x_2x_1,\ x_2y_1,\ x_2,\ y_2x_1,\ y_2y_1,\ y_2,\ x_1,\ y_1,\ 1\big)e=0.$$
Stacking these rows gives $Xe=0$.
**(b)** $E$ has nine entries but the homogeneous scale is irrelevant, leaving eight effective linear unknowns. Eight generic rows leave a one-dimensional null space.
**(c)** The last right singular vector of $X$ gives $\hat E$. If $\hat E=U\operatorname{diag}(\sigma_1,\sigma_2,\sigma_3)V^\top$, project to
$$E^*=U\operatorname{diag}(\bar\sigma,\bar\sigma,0)V^\top,\qquad \bar\sigma=\frac{\sigma_1+\sigma_2}{2}.$$
A mere rank-2 projection is insufficient for an essential matrix because its two non-zero singular values must be equal.

questions.q: With seven correspondences, the linear system has a two-dimensional null space spanned by matrices $E_a,E_b$. (a) Derive the additional cubic constraint for $E(\alpha)=\alpha E_a+E_b$ and state the number of real solutions. (b) Why can the seven-point algorithm return three solutions while the eight-point method is unique? (c) Why does this constraint finish an $F$ estimate but not an $E$ estimate?
questions.answer:
**(a)** The rank-2 condition is
$$\det(E(\alpha))=\det(\alpha E_a+E_b)=0.$$
A $3\times3$ determinant is cubic in its entries and the entries are linear in $\alpha$, so this is a polynomial of degree at most three, with one or three real roots.
**(b)** Eight generic correspondences leave a one-dimensional homogeneous null space and therefore one matrix up to scale. Seven leave a one-parameter family; intersecting it with the cubic rank constraint can produce three matrices.
**(c)** Rank 2 is the only intrinsic algebraic constraint on a fundamental matrix, so each cubic root is a valid $F$. An essential matrix must also have equal non-zero singular values, so a rank-2 root must still be projected onto $\operatorname{diag}(\sigma,\sigma,0)$.

questions.q: Which statements about the eight-point algorithm for relative-pose estimation are correct?
questions.answer: **Correct: 1, 3 and 4.** The same linear construction can estimate $F$ from pixels or $E$ from calibrated rays. One correspondence gives one scalar epipolar constraint. The linear solve temporarily treats the nine matrix entries as independent and uses a norm constraint to exclude the zero vector; rank/essential constraints are enforced afterwards.

options.text: The eight-point algorithm can estimate both essential and fundamental matrices.
Each point correspondence provides two linear constraints on the essential matrix.
The linear algorithm treats the entries of the essential matrix as independent and therefore neglects some inherent constraints.
The linear system is solved with a norm constraint on the unknown vector to avoid the zero solution.

questions.q: For DLT-based estimation, what is the minimum number of 2D-2D point correspondences needed to compute an essential matrix and a homography, respectively?
questions.answer: **Eight** correspondences for the linear essential-matrix estimate and **four** correspondences for a homography. Each homography correspondence supplies two independent linear equations for its eight projective degrees of freedom.

knowledge_points.title: Structure Reconstruction and the Multiple-View Matrix
knowledge_points.recap:
**The scale problem.** $E$, and hence $T$, are only defined up to a positive scale $\gamma$, normalised so that $\|E\|=\|T\|=1$. After recovering $R$ and $T$ we therefore have, for every correspondence $j$,
$$\lambda_2^jx_2^j=\lambda_1^jRx_1^j+\gamma T,\qquad j=1,\dots,n,$$
with the depths $\lambda_i^j$ and the global scale $\gamma$ unknown.
**Linear structure recovery.** Multiplying by $\widehat{x_2^j}$ removes $\lambda_2^j$ (since $\widehat{x_2}x_2=0$), leaving one vector equation per point that is **linear** in $(\lambda_1^1,\dots,\lambda_1^n,\gamma)$. Stacking gives $M\vec\lambda=0$ with $\vec\lambda=(\lambda_1^1,\dots,\lambda_1^n,\gamma)^\top\in\mathbb{R}^{n+1}$ and
$$M=\begin{pmatrix}\widehat{x_2^1}Rx_1^1&0&\cdots&0&\widehat{x_2^1}T\\0&\widehat{x_2^2}Rx_1^2&\cdots&0&\widehat{x_2^2}T\\ \vdots&&\ddots&&\vdots\\0&\cdots&0&\widehat{x_2^n}Rx_1^n&\widehat{x_2^n}T\end{pmatrix}\in\mathbb{R}^{3n\times(n+1)}.$$
Note the hat sits on $x_2$, **not** on $T$; the last column collects the $\gamma$ terms. Solve again by the last right singular vector.
**Multiple views.** For a point seen in $m\ge2$ images with observations $x_1,\dots,x_m$ and projection matrices $\Pi_1,\dots,\Pi_m\in\mathbb{R}^{3\times4}$, define
$$N_p=\begin{pmatrix}\Pi_1&x_1&0&\cdots&0\\ \Pi_2&0&x_2&&0\\ \vdots&&&\ddots&\vdots\\ \Pi_m&0&0&\cdots&x_m\end{pmatrix}\in\mathbb{R}^{3m\times(m+4)}.$$
**Its rank decides existence and uniqueness:**
$\bullet$ $\operatorname{rank}(N_p)=m+4$ (full rank) ⇒ **no** solution;
$\bullet$ $\operatorname{rank}(N_p)=m+3$ ⇒ the solution is **unique** (up to scale);
$\bullet$ $\operatorname{rank}(N_p)<m+3$ ⇒ the solution space has dimension greater than 1 (degenerate configuration, e.g. the point lies on the baseline).
**Three views and coplanarity.** Pairwise epipolar constraints alone are not enough for three views: if $x_1,x_2,x_3$ are **not coplanar**, the pairwise constraints $x_j^\top F_{ij}x_i=0$ do guarantee a unique common preimage.
**2023 paper focus.** For rectified stereo, disparity $d=x_L-x_R$ gives depth $Z=bf/d$, followed by $P=ZK^{-1}\tilde p$. In general two-view triangulation uses known calibrated poses and produces coordinates in the frame in which those poses are expressed.

questions.q: After recovering $R$ and $T$ (with $\|E\|=\|T\|=1$) we have $\lambda_2^jx_2^j=\lambda_1^jRx_1^j+\gamma T$ for $j=1,\dots,n$. To recover the depths in the first camera frame we solve $M\vec\lambda=0$ with $\vec\lambda=(\lambda_1^1,\dots,\lambda_1^n,\gamma)^\top$. Write down $M\in\mathbb{R}^{3n\times(n+1)}$.
questions.answer:
$$M=\begin{pmatrix}\widehat{x_2^1}Rx_1^1&0&\cdots&0&\widehat{x_2^1}T\\0&\widehat{x_2^2}Rx_1^2&\cdots&0&\widehat{x_2^2}T\\ \vdots&&\ddots&&\vdots\\0&0&\cdots&\widehat{x_2^n}Rx_1^n&\widehat{x_2^n}T\end{pmatrix}.$$
**Where it comes from.** Multiplying the $j$-th equation by $\widehat{x_2^j}$ annihilates the left-hand side ($\widehat{x_2}x_2=0$), giving $0=\lambda_1^j\widehat{x_2^j}Rx_1^j+\gamma\widehat{x_2^j}T$ — three scalar equations per point, linear in $\lambda_1^j$ and $\gamma$.
**Structure.** Block-diagonal in the per-point depths (each $\lambda_1^j$ appears in only its own three rows) with a **dense last column** for the shared scale $\gamma$.
questions.extend: The hat goes on $x_2$, never on $T$ — putting it on $T$ costs half a point, as does omitting it entirely.

questions.q: A point $X\in\mathbb{R}^3$ is observed in $m\ge2$ images with observations $x_1,\dots,x_m$ (homogeneous) and projection matrices $\Pi_1,\dots,\Pi_m\in\mathbb{R}^{3\times4}$. For $N_p=\begin{pmatrix}\Pi_1&x_1&0&\cdots&0\\ \Pi_2&0&x_2&&0\\ \vdots&&&\ddots&\vdots\\ \Pi_m&0&0&\cdots&x_m\end{pmatrix}\in\mathbb{R}^{3m\times(m+4)}$, what does the rank of $N_p$ tell you about the existence and uniqueness of a reconstruction $X$?
questions.answer:
**$\operatorname{rank}(N_p)=m+4$ (full rank)** — the only solution is the trivial one, so there are **no** (valid) solutions: the observations are inconsistent, no single 3D point projects to all of them.
**$\operatorname{rank}(N_p)=m+3$** — the null space is one-dimensional, so the reconstruction is **unique** (up to scale). This is the generic, well-posed case.
**$\operatorname{rank}(N_p)<m+3$** — the solution space has dimension greater than 1: the configuration is **degenerate** and the point is not determined (e.g. it lies on the line joining the camera centres).
questions.extend: The $m+4$ unknowns are the 4 homogeneous coordinates of $X$ plus one depth per view; a one-dimensional null space is exactly what a projective point needs.

questions.q: Three cameras have identity rotations and identity intrinsics. With $F_{ij}$ the fundamental matrix between images $i$ and $j$, and pixels $x_1=(10,6,1)^\top$, $x_2=(5,15,1)^\top$, $x_3=(8,9,1)^\top$ satisfying $x_j^\top F_{ij}x_i=0$ for all $i<j$: is it true that "there exists a unique 3D point whose projections in the different images correspond to $x_1,x_2,x_3$"?
questions.answer:
**The statement is true.**
**Explanation.** The vectors $x_1,x_2,x_3$ are **not coplanar**. Together with the pairwise epipolar constraints being satisfied, this guarantees the **existence and uniqueness** of a common preimage: the three viewing rays intersect in exactly one 3D point, so those pixels are indeed the projections of a unique 3D point.
**Why coplanarity matters.** If the three vectors were coplanar, the pairwise constraints could be satisfied without the three rays meeting at a single point — the classic failure of "pairwise consistency does not imply triple consistency", which is what the trifocal tensor / multiple-view matrix is designed to capture.
questions.extend: Two views: the epipolar constraint is necessary and sufficient. Three or more: pairwise constraints alone are **not** sufficient in degenerate (coplanar) configurations.

questions.q: Three cameras have rotations all equal to $I_{3\times3}$; $T_{ij}$ is the translation of the relative pose from camera $i$ to camera $j$ ($1\le i<j\le3$). For the homogeneous pixels $p_1=(10,6,1)^\top$, $p_2=(5,15,1)^\top$, $p_3=(8,9,1)^\top$ of images 1, 2, 3 we know $p_j^\top\widehat{T_{ij}}p_i=0$ for all $i<j$. Is the statement "there exists a unique 3D point whose projections in the different images correspond to $p_1,p_2,p_3$" true, wrong, or impossible to assess? Justify.
questions.answer:
**We cannot assess the validity of the statement in general** — it depends on the intrinsics, and two cases must be distinguished.
**Case 1 — all intrinsics are the identity.** Then $p_j^\top\widehat{T_{ij}}p_i=0$ *is* the pairwise epipolar constraint. Since the vectors $p_1,p_2,p_3$ are **not coplanar**, these constraints ensure the **existence and uniqueness** of the preimage: the pixels are the projections of a unique 3D point, and the statement is **true**.
**Case 2 — some intrinsic matrices are not the identity.** Then the given equations have no significant meaning, because the correct epipolar constraint would be
$$p_j^\top K_j^{-\top}\widehat{T_{ij}}K_i^{-1}p_i=0.$$
The stated equations neither imply nor contradict the existence of a common preimage.
questions.extend: The trap is that the equation *looks* like the epipolar constraint but is only one when $K=I$. Always check whether you are in pixel or normalised coordinates.

questions.q:
With $x_i=(u_i,v_i,1)^\top$ and rows $\pi_{i1}^\top,\pi_{i2}^\top,\pi_{i3}^\top$ of $\Pi_i$:

1. Write the two independent DLT rows for view $i$. (3)
2. State how $X$ is recovered using the SVD. (2)
3. Explain the difference between algebraic error and reprojection error, and why DLT remains useful. (4)
questions.answer:
For view $i$, two independent cross-product equations are
$$(u_i\pi_{i3}^\top-\pi_{i1}^\top)X=0,\qquad(v_i\pi_{i3}^\top-\pi_{i2}^\top)X=0.$$
Stacking all views gives $AX=0$; choose the right singular vector of $A$ associated with its smallest singular value and normalize it homogeneously. DLT minimizes a scale- and parameterization-dependent algebraic residual, not image reprojection error. It remains valuable because it is linear, fast, and supplies a strong initializer for nonlinear geometric refinement.

questions.q: Let $r_1(t)=C_1+td_1$ and $r_2(s)=C_2+sd_2$, with unit directions. Derive the $2\times2$ linear system for $(t^*,s^*)$ minimizing $\|r_1(t)-r_2(s)\|^2$, and give the midpoint estimate. State the degeneracy condition. (9)
questions.answer:
Let $b=C_2-C_1$. The normal equations for the closest points are
$$\begin{bmatrix}d_1^\top d_1&-d_1^\top d_2\\-d_2^\top d_1&d_2^\top d_2\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}t\\s\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}d_1^\top b\\-d_2^\top b\end{bmatrix}.$$
After solving for $(t^*,s^*)$, use
$$X_{mid}=\tfrac12(C_1+t^*d_1+C_2+s^*d_2).$$
For unit directions the determinant is $1-(d_1^\top d_2)^2$, so parallel or nearly parallel rays make triangulation singular or ill-conditioned.
