questions.q: A homogeneous 3D point $X$ is observed as $x_i\sim\Pi_iX$ in $N$ views. Define $W=(\hat x_1\Pi_1;\ldots;\hat x_N\Pi_N)\in\mathbb R^{3N\times4}$. (a) Show that $WX=0$ and $\operatorname{rank}W\le3$, with a geometric interpretation. (b) Why does each $3\times4$ block contribute only two independent equations, and how many views are minimally required?
questions.answer:
Since $\Pi_iX=\lambda_ix_i$,
$$\hat x_i\Pi_iX=\lambda_i(x_i\times x_i)=0.$$
Thus the non-zero vector $X$ is in the null space of every block and of $W$, so $\operatorname{rank}W\le3$. Geometrically, the rank deficiency encodes that all viewing rays are consistent with one common 3D point.
The skew matrix $\hat x_i$ has rank 2 and null space $\operatorname{span}(x_i)$, so $\hat x_i\Pi_i$ contributes at most two independent equations. A homogeneous 3D point has three effective DOF; therefore $2N\ge3$ and at least two views are required in the generic case.

questions.q: For $x_i=(u_i,v_i,1)^\top$ and camera rows $\pi_{i1}^\top,\pi_{i2}^\top,\pi_{i3}^\top$: (a) expand $x_i\times(\Pi_iX)=0$, show that one row is dependent, and assemble the two DLT rows; (b) explain the SVD solution and why it is only algebraically optimal.
questions.answer:
Let $a=\pi_{i1}^\top X$, $b=\pi_{i2}^\top X$, and $c=\pi_{i3}^\top X$. The cross product yields
$$(R1)\ v_ic-b=0,\qquad(R2)\ a-u_ic=0,\qquad(R3)\ u_ib-v_ia=0.$$
But $(R3)=-u_i(R1)-v_i(R2)$, so retain
$$A_i=\begin{pmatrix}u_i\pi_{i3}^\top-\pi_{i1}^\top\\v_i\pi_{i3}^\top-\pi_{i2}^\top\end{pmatrix},\qquad A\in\mathbb R^{2N\times4}.$$
The homogeneous point $X$ is the right singular vector of $A$ with the smallest singular value and is then dehomogenized. This minimizes $\|AX\|$ subject to $\|X\|=1$, an algebraic residual that depends on representation and has no pixel metric. The geometric optimum instead minimizes nonlinear image reprojection error; DLT is valuable as its fast initializer.

questions.q: Two noisy viewing rays are $r_1(t)=C_1+td_1$ and $r_2(s)=C_2+sd_2$. (a) Derive the $2\times2$ system for the closest points and give the midpoint estimate. (b) Is this equivalent to minimizing reprojection error, and what qualitative bias does midpoint triangulation have for a short baseline?
questions.answer:
Let $w=C_1-C_2$ and minimize $\|w+td_1-sd_2\|^2$. Setting both derivatives to zero gives
$$\begin{pmatrix}d_1^\top d_1&-d_1^\top d_2\\-d_1^\top d_2&d_2^\top d_2\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}t^*\\s^*\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}-d_1^\top w\\d_2^\top w\end{pmatrix}.$$
The estimate is
$$X=\frac12\big(r_1(t^*)+r_2(s^*)\big).$$
This minimizes a distance in 3D world coordinates, not 2D pixel reprojection error; perspective projection is nonlinear, so the objectives differ. With a short baseline and nearly parallel rays, midpoint triangulation is depth-insensitive and is biased toward points that are too close to the cameras.

questions.q: Given cameras $\Pi_i$ and points $X_j$, let $\tilde\Pi_i=\Pi_iH^{-1}$ and $\tilde X_j=HX_j$ for any invertible $H\in\mathbb R^{4\times4}$. Verify that all images are unchanged. What extra information reduces the 15-DOF projective ambiguity to a 7-DOF similarity, and then to a 6-DOF Euclidean reconstruction?
questions.answer:
Direct substitution gives
$$\tilde\Pi_i\tilde X_j=\Pi_iH^{-1}HX_j=\Pi_iX_j,$$
so image measurements cannot distinguish reconstructions related by an arbitrary projective transformation $H$ (15 DOF after removing its scale).
Known camera intrinsics calibrate the views, replacing fundamental geometry by essential geometry and reducing the ambiguity to a global similarity: rotation, translation, and scale (7 DOF). One known scene distance or baseline fixes the remaining global scale, leaving a Euclidean reconstruction with only the 6-DOF global rigid-frame ambiguity.

questions.q: Which statements about triangulation from a 2D-2D point correspondence are correct?
questions.answer: **Correct: 2 and 3.** Metric triangulation needs calibrated cameras and known poses. If the camera poses are expressed in a world frame, the reconstructed point is obtained in that frame. The midpoint is specifically associated with the shortest segment between the two rays, not an arbitrary connector, and the standard linear formulation is overdetermined rather than merely well-determined.

options.text: A reconstructed point is the midpoint of an arbitrary 3D line segment connecting the two projection rays.
Known poses and known intrinsic parameters of both cameras are needed for triangulation.
With absolute camera poses in the world frame, the triangulated point is expressed in the world frame.
The mathematical formulation generates a well-determined linear system for the unknown 3D point.

questions.q: A rectified stereo camera has baseline $b=500$ px, focal length $f=800$ px, principal point $(320,240)$, and matched pixels $p=[151,30]^\top$ in the left image and $q=[101,30]^\top$ in the right image. Reconstruct the 3D point in the left-camera frame, in pixels.
questions.answer:
The disparity is $d=x_p-x_q=50$ px, hence
$$Z=\frac{bf}{d}=\frac{500\cdot800}{50}=8000\text{ px}.$$
With
$$K=\begin{pmatrix}800&0&320\\0&800&240\\0&0&1\end{pmatrix},\qquad K^{-1}\tilde p=\begin{pmatrix}-0.21125\\-0.2625\\1\end{pmatrix},$$
the point is
$$P=ZK^{-1}\tilde p=\begin{pmatrix}-1690\\-2100\\8000\end{pmatrix}\text{ px}.$$

knowledge_points.title: The Rotation-Only Case and Estimating R from Correspondences
knowledge_points.recap:
**Setting.** Two cameras whose relative motion is a **pure rotation**: $X_2=RX_1$, with the same known intrinsics $K$.
**The eight-point algorithm fails.** It relies on the epipolar constraint $x_2^\top\hat TRx_1=0$, which becomes **trivial** when $T=0$ ($E=\hat TR=0$). Zero translation means zero parallax, hence no epipolar geometry at all — and there is no "step at which to insert" the constraint.
**What works instead: match directions.** From $\lambda_2p_2=KX_2=KRX_1=KR\lambda_1K^{-1}p_1$ we get, after normalising away the unknown depths,
$$w=Rv\qquad\text{with}\qquad w=\frac{K^{-1}p_2}{\|K^{-1}p_2\|},\quad v=\frac{K^{-1}p_1}{\|K^{-1}p_1\|}.$$
Both the $K^{-1}$ **and** the normalisation are essential: $K^{-1}$ converts pixels to ray directions, and dividing by the norm removes the unknown depth. Normalising $p$ before applying $K^{-1}$ (i.e. $\tfrac{K^{-1}p}{\|p\|}$) is wrong.
**How many correspondences?** A linear map on $\mathbb{R}^n$ is determined by its action on $n$ linearly independent vectors, so in principle $3$ pairs $(v_i,w_i)$ determine $R$. But $R$ preserves the cross product,
$$R(v_1\times v_2)=(Rv_1)\times(Rv_2)=w_1\times w_2,$$
so the third pair comes **for free** from the first two: the **minimal number of 2D–2D correspondences is 2**.
**Closed form.** With $V=[v_1,v_2,v_1\times v_2]$ and $W=[w_1,w_2,w_1\times w_2]$ (both invertible),
$$R=WV^{-1}.$$
Not $V^{-1}W$, not $WV$ — check by applying it to $v_1$.
**With noise.** $WV^{-1}$ will not be exactly orthogonal; project it back onto $SO(3)$ with the SVD, $R^\star=U\operatorname{diag}(1,1,\det(UV^\top))V^\top$ (Chapter 1).

questions.q: Two cameras differ only by an unknown rotation $R\in SO(3)$, i.e. $X_2=RX_1$, with the same known intrinsics $K$. Can the eight-point algorithm be used to estimate $R$? If yes, explain how and at which step the zero-translation constraint must be included; if no, why not?
questions.answer:
**The eight-point algorithm cannot be used.**
**Reason.** It makes use of the **epipolar constraint** $x_2^\top\hat TRx_1=0$, which becomes **trivial** here: with no translation, $T=0$ gives $E=\hat TR=0$, so the constraint reads $0=0$ for every pair of points and carries no information about $R$.
**Consequence.** There is no step at which the zero-translation constraint could be inserted — the entire construction the algorithm rests on has collapsed. One must estimate $R$ directly from ray directions instead.
questions.extend: No translation ⇒ no parallax ⇒ no epipolar geometry. The same degeneracy is why SfM pipelines detect and reject pure-rotation image pairs during initialisation.

questions.q: Let $(p_1,p_2)\in(\mathbb{R}^3)^2$ be a pair of corresponding pixels (homogeneous) for two cameras related by a pure rotation $R$ with shared intrinsics $K$. Which pair of vectors $(w,v)$ fulfils $w=Rv$?
questions.answer:
$$w=\frac{K^{-1}p_2}{\|K^{-1}p_2\|},\qquad v=\frac{K^{-1}p_1}{\|K^{-1}p_1\|}.$$
**Derivation (mirrors the epipolar one).** $\lambda_ip_i=KX_i$ gives $X_i=\lambda_iK^{-1}p_i$; substituting into $X_2=RX_1$ yields $\lambda_2K^{-1}p_2=\lambda_1RK^{-1}p_1$. The depths $\lambda_i$ are unknown, so normalise both sides to unit length — since $R$ preserves norms, the normalised vectors satisfy exactly $w=Rv$.
**Why the others fail.** $K$ (not $K^{-1}$) would go the wrong way, from rays to pixels. Dividing by $\|p_i\|$ instead of $\|K^{-1}p_i\|$ does not produce unit vectors after the $K^{-1}$. And omitting the normalisation leaves the unknown depth ratio in the equation.
questions.extend: $K^{-1}$ first, **then** normalise. The order matters and is exactly what separates the correct option from the decoys.

questions.q: (a) Let $f:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^n$ be a linear transformation. What is the minimum number $N$ of linearly independent vectors $\{v_i\}$ with known images $\{f(v_i)\}$ needed to compute $f(v)$ for any $v\in\mathbb{R}^n$? Justify. (b) For $(w_1,w_2)=(Rv_1,Rv_2)$, express $R(v_1\times v_2)$ in terms of $w_1,w_2$.
questions.answer:
**(a) $N=n$.** We need every $v\in\mathbb{R}^n$ to be expressible as a linear combination of the $\{v_i\}$, i.e. $\operatorname{span}(v_1,\dots,v_N)=\mathbb{R}^n$. Together with linear independence that forces $N=n$ — the vectors must form a basis. Then $f(v)=f(\sum_i\alpha_iv_i)=\sum_i\alpha_if(v_i)$ by linearity.
**(b)**
$$R(v_1\times v_2)=w_1\times w_2.$$
**Consequence.** A rotation preserves the cross product, so knowing the images of $v_1$ and $v_2$ automatically gives the image of $v_1\times v_2$ — the third basis vector comes for free.
questions.extend: That "free third vector" is exactly why a rotation needs only **two** correspondences, not three, even though it is a map on $\mathbb{R}^3$.

questions.q: What is the minimal number of 2D-to-2D correspondences needed to estimate the rotation matrix $R$ between two cameras related by a pure rotation with known intrinsics?
questions.answer:
**2.**
**Why.** Each correspondence gives one pair $(v_i,w_i)$ with $w_i=Rv_i$. A linear map on $\mathbb{R}^3$ would normally need three independent vectors — but since a rotation preserves the cross product, $R(v_1\times v_2)=w_1\times w_2$, the third pair is obtained for free from the first two. Two correspondences therefore already determine a full basis and hence $R$.
**Cross-check with degrees of freedom.** $R$ has 3 DOF and each 2D–2D correspondence provides 2 constraints, so $\lceil3/2\rceil=2$.

questions.q: Let $\{(w_i,v_i)\}$ satisfy $w_i=Rv_i$ for all $i$. Let $W$ have the $w_i$ as columns and $V$ the $v_i$ as columns, both invertible. What is the expression for the rotation matrix $R$?
questions.answer:
$$R=WV^{-1}.$$
**Derivation.** Collecting the relations column-wise gives $W=RV$; right-multiplying by $V^{-1}$ (which exists by assumption) yields $R=WV^{-1}$.
**Check.** $Rv_1=WV^{-1}v_1=We_1=w_1$ ✓.
**In practice.** With noisy measurements $WV^{-1}$ will not be exactly orthogonal — project it back onto $SO(3)$ with the SVD: $R^\star=U\operatorname{diag}\big(1,1,\det(UV^\top)\big)V^\top$.
questions.extend: Order matters: $V^{-1}W$ and $WV$ are both wrong. Verify by applying the candidate to $v_1$ and checking you get $w_1$.

questions.q:
Let $T=0$.

1. What is $E$ and why can it not encode $R$? (2)
2. Derive the image relation $x_2\sim Rx_1$ for calibrated cameras. (2)
3. Form a linear system in the nine entries of $R$ using $x_2\times Rx_1=0$, state the generic number of correspondences needed, and explain how to project the result onto $SO(3)$. (4)
questions.answer:
If $T=0$, then $E=\widehat0R=0$, so the epipolar equation is an identity and contains no information about $R$. Depth cancels directly:
$$x_2\sim Rx_1.$$
Each equation $x_2\times Rx_1=0$ gives two independent linear constraints on the nine entries of $R$. Estimating them up to homogeneous scale generically needs four correspondences. If $\widetilde R=U\Sigma V^\top$, project it to
$$R=U\operatorname{diag}(1,1,\det(UV^\top))V^\top\in SO(3).$$

questions.q:
Embed normalized viewing directions as pure quaternions $p_1,p_2$ and let $p_2=qp_1q^*$.

1. Rearrange this as a homogeneous linear system in $q$ using left/right quaternion multiplication matrices. (4)
2. State how many non-collinear direction correspondences are generically needed. (2)
3. Explain the sign ambiguity of the recovered quaternion. (2)
questions.answer:
From $p_2=qp_1q^*$ and $q^*q=1$, multiply on the right by $q$ to obtain $p_2q=qp_1$. Quaternion left/right multiplication matrices therefore give
$$\bigl(L_{p_2}-R_{p_1}\bigr)q=0.$$
Two non-collinear direction correspondences generically determine the three rotation degrees of freedom. The homogeneous null-space vector is first fixed by unit normalization, but $q$ and $-q$ remain indistinguishable because unit quaternions double-cover $SO(3)$.

questions.q: For pure camera rotation $T=0$: (a) state the essential matrix, whether structure is recoverable, and the image relation; (b) derive the linear matrix approach to estimate $R$ and its minimum correspondence count; (c) derive the quaternion linear system and compare its minimum count.
questions.answer:
**(a)** $E=\hat0R=0$, so the epipolar constraint contains no information. Without a baseline, depth cannot be triangulated; normalized directions satisfy $x_2\sim Rx_1$, a rotation homography.
**(b)** The equation $\hat x_2Rx_1=0$ is linear in the nine entries of $R$. Up to homogeneous scale there are eight unknowns, and each correspondence gives two independent equations, so four generic pairs are needed. If $\hat R=U\Sigma V^\top$, project with
$$R=U\operatorname{diag}(1,1,\det(UV^\top))V^\top.$$
**(c)** Embed directions as pure quaternions. From $p_2=qp_1q^*$, right-multiply by $q$ to get $p_2q=qp_1$, hence
$$(L_{p_2}-R_{p_1})q=0.$$
One pair leaves rotation around that direction free; two non-collinear pairs generically leave a one-dimensional null space. Normalize the recovered $q$. This uses two correspondences and four unknowns instead of four correspondences and nine matrix entries.
